AI Security Is Becoming a Serious Concern

AI is quickly moving from simple chatbots to autonomous AI agents that can browse websites, execute code, access files, call APIs, use MCP tools, and interact with real business systems. As AI gets permission to do more, security becomes much more important because a compromised agent could potentially take an unwanted action instead of simply generating a wrong answer.

Prompt Injection  The Hidden AI Attack

One of the biggest concerns in AI security is Prompt Injection. Malicious instructions can be hidden inside websites, emails, documents, code, or other content an AI agent processes. If the system doesn't properly separate trusted instructions from untrusted content, this can lead to unintended behavior, tool calls, or sensitive-data exposure.

AI Agents Have Access to Sensitive Systems

Modern AI agents can connect to browsers, terminals, databases, APIs, emails, MCP servers, and company data. This creates a larger attack surface. A security issue could potentially move across multiple connected components—from external content to an AI agent, then to a tool or API, and finally to sensitive systems.

Autonomous AI Creates New Security Challenges

The more autonomy we give an AI agent, the more carefully its permissions need to be controlled. Browser agents, coding agents, and computer-use agents can perform real actions, so sandboxing, least-privilege access, authentication, monitoring, and approval for sensitive actions become important security layers.

Vibe Coders  Security Matters

If you're using AI to quickly build applications, don't ignore security just because the code works. API keys, .env files, database credentials, authentication tokens, and private user data should never be accidentally exposed in client-side code or public repositories. AI generated code should still be reviewed and tested before production deployment.

Build AI Agents Securely

In this video, we'll understand AI Security, Prompt Injection, Agent Hijacking, MCP Security, API Key Security, tool permissions, sandboxing, and data protection in simple Tamil. As AI moves from “Generate an Answer”-“Take an Action,” building secure systems becomes an essential part of working with AI agents.

videos.title: The Psychology of People Who Don't Post on Social Media (Explained by a Neuroscientist)
videos.description:
People who never post aren't shy or too cool for it. Most of them were TRAINED into silence.

Every like, every notification, every post that flopped has been quietly shaping how much you share, WHAT you share, and whether you share AT ALL. And the research shows that just scrolling and watching comes with its own cost. In this video I break down what's actually going on in your brain, and give you simple ways to take some control back.

By the end you'll know which type of poster you are according to science, what trained you into it, and why the best thing you can do on these apps might be to post anyway. 

---
REFERENCES

The Four Posting Types:
A questionnaire of 835 young people in Spain, Chile and Colombia that sorted them into four posting types based on how often and what they post. (Rodríguez-Illera et al. (2021), Pixel-Bit)
Link: https://doi.org/10.12795/pixelbit.74205

How Likes Change What We Post:
An online experiment where 248 users got more or fewer likes than expected on a simulated post. More likes made people want to post sooner; fewer made them change what they'd post next. (Stsiampkouskaya et al. (2021), Computers in Human Behavior)
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2021.106940

Viewing selfies vs. group photos:
A survey of 275 people linking frequent selfie viewing to lower self-esteem and group photo viewing to higher self-esteem. Posting had no effect. (Wang, Yang & Haigh (2017), Telematics and Informatics)
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tele.2016.07.004

Additional background references: 

1. The foundational work on reinforcement and extinction. (Skinner (1938), The Behavior of Organisms)
2. Shows dopamine responds to the gap between what we expect and what we get. (Schultz, Dayan & Montague (1997), Science)
https://doi.org/10.1126/science.275.5306.1593
3. The original theory of how we judge ourselves by comparing to others. (Festinger (1954), Human Relations)
https://doi.org/10.1177/001872675400700202

--
I'm Dr. Sahar Yousef, a cognitive neuroscientist and MBA Faculty at UC Berkeley, where I run the Becoming Superhuman Lab. My goal is to make neuroscience accessible and actionable for anyone looking for better ways of living and working. Everything on this channel is built on the realities of how your brain and body actually work.

videos.title: Robot-Use Agents: Why General-Purpose Models May Win in Robotics
videos.description:
One of the biggest surprises in AI over the last few years has been how well coding agents generalize beyond software. In a recent essay, MIT professor Philip Isola argued that we may be entering the era of robot-use agents: general-purpose models that can control different robots, write policies, and learn new physical tasks with little or no robot-specific training.

In this episode of Decoded, we're joined by the founders of Waddle Labs and RoboCurve, two of the startups whose work helped drive this realization. They're working at the frontier of using general-purpose models to control robots, and their recent demos helped inspire the growing conversation around robot-use agents. 

Together, we dig into the research behind that idea, from code-as-policies and vision-language-action models to the harnesses and evals needed to make these systems work in the real world.

Gary Vaynerchuk is a serial entrepreneur and serves as the Chairman of VaynerX, the CEO of VaynerMedia, and the CEO and creator of VeeFriends. Gary is considered one of the leading global minds on what's next in culture, business, and the internet.

Known as "GaryVee," he is described as one of the most forward thinkers in business. He acutely recognizes trends and patterns early to help others understand how shifts in consumer attention impact the realities of the business world today. Gary's approach sits at the intersection of business and pop culture. He keenly understands how to bring brand relevance to the forefront. He is a prolific angel investor with early investments in companies like Facebook, Twitter, Tumblr, Venmo, Snapchat, Coinbase, and Uber.

Gary is an entrepreneur at heart – he builds businesses. Today, he helps Fortune 1000 brands leverage consumer attention through his full-service advertising agency, VaynerMedia, which has offices in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Miami, Toronto, Mexico City, London, Amsterdam, Sydney, Singapore, Tokyo, Bangkok, Delhi, and Kuala Lumpur. He is a six-time New York Times bestselling author, with titles including Crush It!, Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook, Twelve and a Half and Day Trading Attention. In addition to running multiple businesses, Gary documents his daily life as a CEO through his social media channels, which have more than 45 million followers and garner more than 300 million monthly impressions/views across all platforms. His podcast, "The GaryVee Audio Experience," ranks among the top podcasts globally.

Gary serves on the board of MikMak, Bojangles Restaurants, Global Citizen Forum, The Paley Center, and Pencils of Promise. He is also a longtime Well Member of charity: water.

Gary's life ambition is to buy the New York Jets.
